turn_text: Talking about the fire is a good segue into an issue that you know well. You were the state's first elected insurance commissioner. Certainly the issue of people being able to ensure their homes is a fundamental issue with the state right now, one that we hear every day from every place. Talk a little bit about what you're seeing and what you think needs to be done.

I would put two things on the agenda here. One is the appropriate regulation of the insurance industry. And that was laid out in Proposition 103 in 1998 as a result of an automobile insurance crisis. I became the first elected insurance commissioner as a result of that initiative. And we set about a process to regulate the insurance industry to bring it into a rational economic situation in which they could earn a decent profit and they could provide the necessary insurance and services to homeowners auto insurance and the like in California. We did it and it worked. Unfortunately, in the current situation, the insurance commissioner simply has not used the powers that are available to him under the law And in fact, he's given up too many of those powers to the insurance companies. And he's allowed the insurance companies to basically run unregulated across the state of California and giving to them whatever they think they need, not what they must have. What they must have is a stable market situation in which they can assess their risk and charge a price for insurance that is reasonable given the risks that they have. extensive hearings and studies of the individual insurance companies so that the insurance policies are properly priced, fair to the consumers, and meet the needs of the insurance companies to pay claims when and where a claim is required, and also that the claims be paid fairly and promptly. Now, having said all of that, if the insurance commissioner were to do that, most of this problem could be solved and the consumers would know what is going on. Right now, we really don't. And I follow it very closely and simply do not know what a reasonable level of policy would be necessary and at what cost there is a problem that we were addressing in the early 90s. And again, in 2000, I became the Insurance Commissioner once again. And that is the extraordinary occurrences that do happen across this nation. And these are the disasters. Normally, they are the disasters of weather, floods, hurricanes, tornadoes, earthquakes. I guess that's not weather, but nonetheless, a natural disaster. Those disasters are the extraordinary events that can destabilize the entire insurance market. We tried for, well, that was 16 years, that period of time, to put in place a national natural disaster insurance program in which the risk would be spread out across the entire nation, not just in one location, for example, southern Florida. or tornado alley or earthquake California. So that is something we should continue to pursue because the insurance systems simply are not capable of handling those extraordinary expenses. Now the firestorm in Southern California could very well be such a natural disaster and obviously going to be extraordinarily expensive. The result of that is going to be a destabilized insurance market in California, and also it's going to be one in which tens of thousands of policyholders are going to be facing a very, very difficult claims situation, one that needs to be managed by the insurance commissioner. So we'll see what goes down here. Going forward by plea to the commissioner is transparency. Make things companies come in. make them show the books, show their losses, show the risks out there, hold them to account. And if they need an increase in their premiums, okay, make sure it's reasonable. And over time, when I was commissioner, we were able to do that. We stabilized the market and things settled down. However, right now it's going to be difficult for Californians and certainly the commissioner has an extraordinary task to do. And I just hope that he takes it seriously and does his job.
